No.56

What Does It Mean to Learn "With Heart"?

Learning with heart is not straining but truly being present: focus, reflection and practice, so that what we learn truly transforms us.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

🔶 I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva: "I often hear people say 'learn with your heart' (用心學習). What exactly does this 'heart' mean?"

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

"Good man,
you now ask:
the world often says,
'learn with your heart'.
But what, in the end, is this heart?
Is it the heart beating in the chest?
Is it the thought thinking in the brain?
Is it the consciousness that remembers and discriminates?

Or is it the mind of which the Dharma speaks?
I will now make it clear for you.
The heart is not one thing;
it cannot be sought by clinging to one place.
What the world calls using the heart
mostly means focus, reflection,
understanding, memory and will.
Yet seen through the Dharma,
the workings of the mind
do not stop there.

The eye sees forms,
the ear hears sounds,
the mind can reflect,
consciousness can discriminate.
Meeting things, joy arises;
meeting adversity, anger arises;
seeing good, one wishes to do it;
seeing evil, one wishes to avoid it.

All these activities of body and mind
are bound up with mind and consciousness.
Yet you must know:
to be able to think
is not necessarily to use the heart;
to be able to remember
is not necessarily true learning.
Some read a sutra a thousand times,
seeking only to recite the words fluently,
not reflecting on the Dharma within it,
nor looking at themselves.

Some hear a single line of Dharma,
reflect on it again and again,
and in daily life
gradually lessen their afflictions.
Of what these two have learned,
which enters the heart more?
Therefore I say:
using the heart is not only committing knowledge to memory,
but letting what you learn truly change you.

If you learn a teaching,
there should be three levels.
First, the mind can settle.
When reading a sutra, know you are reading a sutra;
when hearing the Dharma, know you are hearing the Dharma.
Do not let distraction pull you,
nor follow wandering thoughts as they race.
This is focus.

Second, the mind can reflect.
Hearing the meaning of a teaching,
do not merely accept it,
but ask its cause,
examine its principle,
and discern whether it accords
with the scriptures and with reality.
This is discernment.

Third, the mind can practice.
One who knows compassion
should practice compassion in dealing with people.
One who knows impermanence
should cling less in gain and loss.
One who knows cause and effect
should act with care
when thoughts and intentions arise.

This is practice.
Focus keeps the mind from scattering,
reflection makes the principle gradually clear,
practice lets the Dharma enter the body.
If you seek only focus
without discerning right and wrong,
then focus too may
be used for unwholesome things.

If you seek only knowledge
without being willing to practice,
then though you know much,
your afflictions may not lessen.
So the heart of which Buddhist learning speaks
is not only concentration;
it must also have wisdom.
Not only wisdom;
it must also have compassion.

Good man,
you should also know:
the heart is not a master that never changes.
Today's heart
and yesterday's heart
arise and pass with every thought.
They arise because of circumstances,
and turn according to conditions.

One thought of joy,
one thought of sorrow;
one thought of compassion,
one thought of envy.
If you cling to one of these thoughts
and take it to be
an eternal true self,
confusion arises again.

The Dharma's way of looking at the mind
is not only searching for
'where the mind is',
but observing:
how does the mind arise?
Why does it grasp?
How does it suffer?
And how are the causes of suffering brought to rest?

Knowing how the mind arises,
you can observe how it changes;
knowing the mind is impermanent,
you are not bound by the mind.
For example, when you recite the Diamond Sutra
and hear 'Let the mind arise without abiding anywhere',
it does not teach you
not to think,
not to feel,
nor teach you
to become a person without thoughts.

Rather it urges you:
when doing good,
do not cling to merit;
when dealing with people,
do not cling to reward;
when learning the Dharma,
do not cling to the idea
that you are already above others.

The heart may act,
yet need not cling everywhere.
If you ask:
'What, after all, is using the heart?'
I will tell you by one example.
When someone speaks to you,
though you hear their voice,
your mind thinks only
of how to refute them —
this is hearing with the ear,
not necessarily listening with the heart.

If you can set your own views aside for a while,
listen carefully to their meaning,
understand their suffering,
and then respond with wisdom —
this is using the heart.
Some read sutras
and only count how many scrolls they recited today;
this is one side of diligence,
but not the whole.

If, reading a line,
you suddenly see in yourself
your everyday greed and anger,
and are willing to correct them,
this is the Dharma entering your heart.
Using the heart is not the heart straining hard,
but the heart truly being present.
It is not gripping every thought,
but knowing clearly
what you are doing.

It is not that the more you think about everything,
the more you use your heart.
Overthinking
can also become an obstacle.
Sometimes using the heart
is thinking earnestly;
sometimes using the heart
is letting go of scattered thoughts;
sometimes using the heart
is listening attentively;
sometimes using the heart
is seeing your own attachment
and being willing to let it go.

Good man,
I tell you once more:
if the mind is scattered,
learning hardly enters;
if the mind is attached,
learning hardly flows through;
if the mind is clear,
learning can discern;
if the mind is compassionate,
learning can be lived.

So learning with the heart
is not only seeking knowledge;
it is learning
how to use your own heart.
Gather the mind with right mindfulness,
discern principles with wisdom,
treat people with compassion,
confirm it with action.

Finally, in four lines,
I urge you:
using the heart is not using force;
focus is not attachment;
hearing the Dharma, reflect on its meaning;
understanding the principle, put it into practice.
And also:
the heart lies not in seeking its form,
but in seeing how it works;
learning lies not in knowing much,
but in whether it can turn your heart.

Good man,
if today you hear one teaching
and tomorrow give rise to a little less anger;
if today you understand one principle
and tomorrow practice a little more compassion,
this is
the good fruit
that truly learning with heart can bear."

🔶Plain Rendering

Good man,
you now ask:
people often say "learn with your heart".
But what exactly is this "heart"?
Is it the heart beating in your chest?
Is it the thoughts in your head?
Is it the consciousness that remembers and tells things apart?
Or is it the mind that the Dharma speaks of?

I will make it clear for you now. The heart is not one fixed thing; you cannot cling to one place and look for it there. When people talk about using their heart, they mostly mean focus, thinking, understanding, memory and willingness. But from the Dharma's point of view, the workings of the mind go beyond this. The eyes see forms, the ears hear sounds, the mind can think, consciousness can tell things apart.

When things go well, joy arises;
when things go badly, anger arises;
seeing good, we want to do it;
seeing harm, we want to avoid it.
All these activities of body and mind
are connected with the mind and consciousness.
But you must know:
being able to think does not necessarily mean using your heart;
being able to remember does not necessarily mean truly learning.

Some people read a sutra a thousand times,
only trying to memorize the words,
without thinking about the meaning of the teaching,
or looking at themselves.
Some people hear one line of the Dharma,
think it over again and again,
and gradually have fewer afflictions in daily life.
Of what these two people have learned,
which goes deeper into the heart?

So I say:
using your heart is not only memorizing knowledge,
but letting what you learn truly change you.
When you learn a teaching,
there should be three levels.
First, the mind can settle.
When reading a sutra, know you are reading a sutra;
when listening to the Dharma, know you are listening to the Dharma.

Do not let the mind be pulled along by distraction,
or go racing after wandering thoughts.
This is focus.
Second, the mind can reflect.
When you hear a teaching,
do not just accept it;
ask why,
look at the reasoning behind it,
and check whether it fits the scriptures and real life.

This is discernment.
Third, the mind can put it into practice.
If you know about compassion,
show compassion when dealing with people.
If you know about impermanence,
cling less when you gain or lose.
If you know about cause and effect,
act carefully whenever an intention arises.

This is practice.
Focus keeps the mind from scattering,
reflection makes the teaching gradually clearer,
practice brings the Dharma into your life.
If you only seek focus
without telling right from wrong,
focus may also be used for harmful things.
If you only seek knowledge
but are not willing to practice,
then even though you know a lot,
your afflictions may not lessen.

So the heart that Buddhist learning speaks of
is not only about concentration; it also needs wisdom.
Not only wisdom; it also needs compassion.
Good man,
you should also know:
the heart is not a master that never changes.
Today's heart
and yesterday's heart
arise and pass away thought by thought.

They arise with circumstances
and change with conditions.
One thought is joyful,
one thought is sad;
one thought is compassionate,
one thought is jealous.
If you cling to one of these thoughts
and believe it is your eternal true self,
you become confused again.

The Dharma's way of looking at the mind
is not only searching for "where the mind is",
but also observing:
how does the mind arise?
Why does it grasp?
How does it suffer?
And how can the causes of suffering be stopped?
Knowing how the mind arises, you can see how it changes;
knowing the mind is impermanent, you will not be bound by it.

For example, when you recite the Diamond Sutra and hear "Let the mind arise without abiding anywhere", it is not teaching you to stop thinking or stop feeling, nor to become a person without thoughts. It is urging you: when doing good, do not cling to merit; when dealing with people, do not cling to getting something back; when learning the Dharma, do not cling to the idea that you are already better than others.

The heart can act, but it does not need to cling everywhere. If you ask: "So what exactly counts as using my heart?" I will tell you with one example. When someone is talking to you, you hear their voice, but your mind is only thinking about how to argue back — that is hearing with the ears, not necessarily listening with the heart.

If you can set your own views aside for a moment,
listen carefully to what they mean,
understand their pain,
and then respond with wisdom,
that is using your heart.
Some people read sutras
and only count how many scrolls they recited today;
this is part of diligence,
but not all of it.

If, reading a certain line,
you suddenly see your own everyday greed and anger,
and are willing to change,
that is the Dharma entering your heart.
Using your heart is not straining hard,
but your heart truly being present.
It is not gripping every thought,
but knowing clearly what you are doing.

It is not that the more you think about everything, the more you use your heart. Overthinking can also become an obstacle. Sometimes using your heart means thinking seriously; sometimes it means letting go of scattered thoughts; sometimes it means listening attentively; sometimes it means seeing your own attachment and being willing to let it go. Good man, I tell you again: if the mind is scattered, learning hardly sinks in; if the mind is attached, learning hardly gets through; if the mind is clear, learning lets you discern; if the mind is compassionate, learning lets you act.

So learning with your heart
is not only seeking knowledge,
but learning how to use your own heart.
Gather the mind with right mindfulness,
discern the teaching with wisdom,
treat others with compassion,
and confirm what you learn through action.
Finally, I urge you in four lines:
using the heart is not using force;
focus is not attachment;
hearing the Dharma, reflect on its meaning;
understanding the principle, put it into practice.

And also:
the heart is not about seeking its shape,
but about seeing how it works;
learning is not about how much you know,
but about whether it can transform your heart.
Good man,
if today you hear one teaching
and tomorrow you get a little less angry,
if today you understand one principle
and tomorrow you act with a little more compassion,
that is the good fruit
that truly learning with your heart can bear.
